detail: The three-modality recommendation and fetal-specific settings appear together in the Section III Key Points, p. 697. III.A, Equipment, p. 683 describes system capabilities.
III.A, Equipment, p. 683 makes CW Doppler an option for characterising high velocities when available. The claim changes a permitted use to a categorical description.

III.A, Equipment, p. 683 recommends a 2–7 MHz range for late second- and third-trimester scanning. The 5–12 MHz range for the earlier window is a possible aid. The claim treats the first range as merely suitable.

III.B, Acoustic Bioeffects, p. 684 applies ALARA to fetal echocardiographic studies. It says operators should be aware of TI and MI and limit power and exposure time. “Every fetal study” broadens the scope beyond the examination discussed.

III.D, Image Optimization, p. 684 gives the higher 80–100 Hz range for capturing important events at heart rates above 140 beats/min or for speckle tracking. “Faster” omits the stated threshold. The baseline frame rate and adjustment techniques agree.

III.A, Storage, p. 684 says the study should include stills, motion and a structured report. It requires an abdominal-stomach to upper-mediastinal sweep and both 2D and colour clips for the named individual views, including both 3VV and 3VT. The claim drops the mode requirements.

The view-specific uses appear in III.E, four-chamber view, p. 687, LV outflow tract, p. 688, and RV outflow, 3VT, bicaval and short-axis views, p. 689. Table 3, p. 686 also assigns colour to atrial and ventricular septal assessment. III.G alone does not enumerate these uses.
III.G, Color and Power Doppler Ultrasound, p. 689 covers amplitude, direction, smaller vessels and low velocities. III.D, Image Optimization, p. 684 supplies the septal-defect application.

III.G, PW Doppler Ultrasound, p. 689 specifies alignment along flow or an angle strictly below 20°, excluding 20°. A small gate reduces the chance of sampling multiple sites. It does not guarantee a single-site signal.

Table 6, p. 693 includes great arteries as well as arches (transverse aortic segment and isthmus) in the optional row. The annular sites are lateral tricuspid/mitral and the combined LV recording is for IVRT. III.G, PW Doppler, p. 689 includes arches generically among minimum sites without separately naming the aortic arch and isthmus. See the accompanying ruling.

III.G, CW Doppler Ultrasound, p. 692 gives the normal-heart qualification, alignment, stenosis gradients and ventricular pressure estimation from the corresponding AV regurgitant jet. III.A, Equipment, p. 683 explicitly addresses high velocities.
The requirement to document the mechanism and the three modalities are in IV.A, Rhythm Disturbances and Tools for Assessment, Key Points, p. 699. Page 697 introduces the tools.
Figure 11F, p. 697 shows the atrial-wall and ventricular-free-wall cursor. IV.A, p. 699 explains that the high temporal resolution enables precise timing of atrial and ventricular contraction.

IV.A, p. 699 specifies both lateral annuli for myocardial velocities and timing. Figure 11D, p. 697 shows the tricuspid site. Table 9, p. 698 specifically identifies lateral tricuspid tissue Doppler as a possible aid in sinus bradycardia.

III.I, Alternative Ultrasound Modalities, p. 693 discusses tissue Doppler and strain jointly for assessing myocardial mechanics. It attributes detection of subclinical dysfunction specifically to 2D strain/speckle tracking. Their application in pregnancy needs further investigation.
Introduction, p. 788 says the listed measures can improve programme performance. The claim states the performance benefit without that qualification.

Technical factors, Zoom, cine-loop and image storage, p. 789 also calls for appropriate patient identification in the clinical examination record and consideration of local or national archiving standards. Laterality and orientation labels alone do not cover its documentation instructions.

Four-chamber view, p. 792 describes an association between transient bradycardia and probe pressure. “Often from” strengthens that association to a cause. The persistent rate threshold, well-fetus qualifier, referral and listed possible causes agree.

Four-chamber view, p. 792 advises displaying colour alongside B-mode in the passage about showing pulmonary veins entering the left atrium. The claim turns this into a rule for every use of colour Doppler.

Four-chamber view, p. 793 says abnormal AV valve alignment can be a key sonographic finding in anomalies such as AV septal defect. The claim makes it categorical. The normal offset and valve-opening descriptions agree.
RVOT view, 3VV and 3VTV, p. 794 describes greater reliability of live or cine review as likely. The claim states it without that qualification. Figure 8 on p. 795 illustrates the continuum.
RVOT view, 3VV and 3VTV, last paragraph on p. 794, gives the position cephalad to the 3VV. The paragraph resumes on p. 796 with the obliquity and vessel/trachea anatomy. See also Figure 9, p. 796.

Color flow Doppler ultrasound, p. 796 recommends the two stated velocity scales. It describes low colour persistence as ordinarily built into cardiac presets, without giving it the same direct instruction as the scale setting.

Table 2, Fetal factors, p. 797 specifies a suspected cardiac structural anomaly. An extracardiac structural anomaly is an indication here when it has a known association with CHD. The unqualified first item broadens referral.

Table 2, Patient or familial disease or environmental exposure, p. 797 explicitly includes parents, siblings and half-siblings in its first family-history entry. Reporting only the degree loses the table’s explicit inclusion of half-siblings.

Table 2, Other considerations, p. 797 qualifies non-cardiac soft markers as markers for aneuploidy, fever as prenatal, and the distant relative’s isolated disease as congenital. Its BMI threshold is ≥35 kg/m². The evidence statement concerns risk of CHD.

Fetal echocardiography, p. 797 includes familiarity with postnatal management and prognosis in the specialist’s qualifications, alongside prenatal diagnosis and postnatal course. The claim drops those two elements. Its maternal-distress statement is supported.

Early fetal cardiac screening, p. 798 specifies bidirectional flow mapping when describing high-quality power Doppler. The claim allows unspecified power Doppler. The transabdominal and transvaginal probe statements agree.

Early fetal cardiac screening, p. 798, items 2 and 3 and Figure 10, specifies colour and/or bidirectional power Doppler for the four-chamber and three-vessel-and-trachea views. Omitting bidirectionality changes the accepted power mode.

Early fetal cardiac screening, p. 798 specifies suspicion of congenital heart disease at the early scan as the referral trigger. “Any suspicion” is broader. The limitations of early outflow views are supported.
